extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants and practitioners (inventors, agents, attorneys) interacting with the USPTO
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the types of official USPTO letters (office actions, notices), the required content and form of replies, applicable deadlines, acceptable filing methods, and consequences of failing to respond. Targets handling patent prosecution correspondence with the USPTO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office Action (response requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Office Action - written correspondence from the patent examiner requiring a properly signed written response from you in order for prosecution of your application to continue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include a restriction requirement, a non-final office action, and a final office action. Your reply must address each ground of rejection and objection the examiner has made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice of Allowability (PTOL-37)
rubrics_metrics.description: Notice of Allowability - a USPTO form (PTOL-37) is mailed to you if the patent examiner determines that all pending claims in the application are allowable (eligible to receive a patent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The notice identifies the allowable claims and the required fees to be paid before a patent is issued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notices identifying deficiencies (e.g., Non‑Compliant Amendment)
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner may mail another type of notice identifying any deficiencies in the application or your correspondence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You usually have two months to correct the deficiency unless the notice accompanies an office action. An example of such a notice is a Notice of Non-Compliant Amendment. (For a Notice to File Missing Parts or a Notice of Incomplete Application, learn more on the USPTO webpage covering applications that are incomplete or missing information.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Response deadlines and statutory timing
rubrics_metrics.description: By law, most replies to office actions (official letters) must be received within six months from the date the office action was mailed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office actions almost always shorten the time period within which you can file a response without paying an extension-of-time fee. The shortened period is typically either two or three months, depending on the type of office action, with different response periods in certain circumstances. There are no extensions to the six-month legal reply window other than for notices without such a limit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable submission methods and filing date rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Submit replies to office actions and other official letters via Patent Center (registered eFilers only), postal mail, fax to the official USPTO fax number (571-273-8300), or hand-carried to the USPTO customer service window in Alexandria, Virginia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Electronic responses submitted in Patent Center (registered eFilers only) receive an Eastern Time stamp; any submission arriving by 11:59 p.m. ET will be granted that day's filing date. Postal-mailed responses with sufficient postage, sent as first-class mail and deposited with the USPS will receive the benefit of the date of deposit for timeliness purposes if accompanied by a signed, completed certificate of mailing. Responses faxed to the official USPTO fax number will be credited with the date of transmission if a signed, completed certificate of transmission accompanies it. You should keep a copy of the response with the signed certificate in case the response is lost or not received by the USPTO. Responses mailed to the USPTO from outside the United States or hand-carried to the customer service window will be credited with the actual date they are received.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of failing to timely submit an acceptable response
rubrics_metrics.description: If you do not submit an acceptable, timely response to an office action or other official letter, your application will be abandoned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because office actions often impose shortened response periods and the six-month statutory window has limited extensions, timely and acceptable replies are necessary to avoid abandonment.
